overview: Muttaburrasaurus langdoni was a large ornithopod from the Early to Late Cretaceous of Queensland, Australia (~100 Ma), reaching about seven metres. It is the most completely known dinosaur from Australia, and its inflated nasal region — forming a distinctive hollow crest or bulge on the snout — may have amplified calls or enhanced the sense of smell.

Australia was an isolated continent during the Cretaceous, separated from Antarctica and South America, and its dinosaur fauna is consequently distinctive. Muttaburrasaurus is an iguanodontian without close relatives in the Northern Hemisphere, illustrating the independent evolution of large ornithopods on the southern Gondwanan landmasses.

fossilSites.name: Mackunda Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Cretaceous (Albian–Cenomanian) fluvial deposits with the most complete Muttaburrasaurus specimen, found near Muttaburra in 1963.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Doug Langdon found the first Muttaburrasaurus skeleton near the Flinders River in Queensland in 1963. Ralph Molnar and Alan Bartholomai described it formally in 1981. A second specimen from White Mountains, Queensland has provided additional skull material, and isolated teeth and bones are known from South Australia and possibly New South Wales.

articles.title: Nasal crest
articles.body: The inflated nasal region may have been covered by soft tissue forming a resonating chamber for vocalisation — analogous (though not homologous) to the hollow crests of hadrosaurs like Parasaurolophus. Alternatively it may have housed enlarged nasal passages for enhanced olfaction. No soft tissue is preserved, so the function remains hypothetical.

articles.title: Australian Cretaceous context
articles.body: Cretaceous Australia was separated from other continents and straddled the Antarctic Circle, experiencing months of polar darkness each year. Muttaburrasaurus and other Australian Cretaceous dinosaurs lived in cool, possibly dark winters, suggesting dinosaurs were physiologically capable of tolerating harsh seasonal conditions far better than a cold-blooded reptile could.

fossilRecord.material: A nearly complete skull and partial postcranial skeleton plus isolated teeth from other sites.
fossilRecord.paleo: Early Cretaceous of eastern Australia, when a shallow inland sea covered much of the continent.
fossilRecord.evidence: The inflated nasal region and unusual shearing teeth distinguish it from other ornithopods and suggest a specialised diet.

record.mya: late Albian-Cenomanian, about 105-100 million years ago
record.description: Muttaburrasaurus langdoni was a large Australian ornithopod known from two partial skeletons and additional bones, including two skulls. Recent analyses place it among early-diverging iguanodontians, often close to Rhabdodontomorpha.
facts: The holotype and second skull differ in ways that may reflect variation, deformation or taxonomy.
The enlarged nasal region is preserved, but a resonating or display function is speculative.
Herbivory is secure; a special omnivorous diet proposed from tooth form is not established.

review.ageReviewNote: Material comes from upper Albian to Cenomanian units; the old 112-99 Ma span is too broad.

sources.citation: Bartholomai & Molnar (1981), original description of Muttaburrasaurus
Dieudonne et al. (2021), phylogenetic relationships of Muttaburrasaurus and rhabdodontomorphs

residualUncertainty: The two principal skulls need renewed comparative study.
Fine phylogenetic position and nasal function remain unsettled.

evidence.material: Two partial skeletons with skulls plus isolated referred remains.
evidence.formations: Mackunda and Allaru formations, Queensland, Australia.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Nasal display, vocalisation and omnivory are unsupported hypotheses.
